profile.summary: ProtSSN scores the effect of amino acid substitutions on a protein without any experimental training data for that protein (zero-shot). It takes a protein sequence together with its 3D structure as a PDB file and returns a fitness score for each listed mutant. It combines a protein language model for the sequence with a graph neural network over the structure, and needs no multiple sequence alignment.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: Introduction; Prepare Your Own Dataset. Paper: Abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each protein is turned into a k-nearest-neighbour graph over its residues. A frozen ESM2-t33 language model supplies the node features, and a six-layer equivariant graph neural network (EGNN) learns from the structure. Pre-training is a denoising task: residues are randomly mutated at each epoch to imitate natural mutation, and the model learns to recover the wild type. Variant effects are then scored from the model's fitness for the mutated sequence. The authors describe the method as an adapter that strengthens a language model, and the language model can be swapped.

sections.body: Nine checkpoints are released, one for each combination of graph size k (10, 20 or 30 neighbours) and hidden size h (512, 768 or 1280). They are named k10_h512 to k30_h1280. They can be used alone or averaged as an ensemble; the developers recommend k20_h512 when using one model. A result should name the checkpoint, or the list of checkpoints in the ensemble. The Hugging Face repository was at revision cb2d622f when read.

sections.title: Inputs and data preparation
sections.body: Each protein needs a folder with its PDB structure and a TSV file of mutants. Multiple mutations in one variant are joined with a colon, for example M1V:A2V. The developers suggest predicting the structure with AlphaFold or ESMFold, or downloading it from the AlphaFold database. A helper script builds all single-point saturation mutants for a protein that has no experimental data.

profile.summary: xTrimoPGLM is a family of protein language models that handles both understanding and generation. One pretraining framework combines a masked (autoencoding) objective with an autoregressive one, so the same design yields masked models that embed and classify sequences and causal models that write new ones. The published family runs from 1 billion to 100 billion parameters, the largest trained on 1 trillion tokens. A masked model takes an amino acid sequence and returns per-residue embeddings or mask predictions; a causal model continues a sequence prompt.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The family is built on the GLM transformer design, as the ProteinGLM model and config classes show: the released 1B masked model has 24 layers, hidden size 2048, 32 attention heads and a vocabulary of 128 tokens. The contribution the paper claims is joint optimisation of two pretraining objectives, autoencoding and autoregressive, in one model. In the released code a single configuration flag, is_causal, switches a checkpoint between masked use and causal use, and the loading class decides whether the output is mask predictions, a sequence label, per-token labels or generated text.

steps.title: Get residue embeddings from the 1B masked model
steps.shell:
python3 - <<'PY'
from transformers import AutoModelForMaskedLM, AutoTokenizer
import torch

tokenizer  = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("Bo1015/proteinglm-1b-mlm", trust_remote_code=True, use_fast=True)
model = AutoModelForMaskedLM.from_pretrained("Bo1015/proteinglm-1b-mlm",  trust_remote_code=True, torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16)
if torch.cuda.is_available():
    model = model.cuda()
model.eval()

seq = 'MILMCQHFSGQFSKYFLAVSSDFCHFVFPIILVSHVNFKQMKRKGFALWNDRAVPFTQGIFTTVMILLQYLHGTG'
output = tokenizer(seq, add_special_tokens=True, return_tensors='pt')
with torch.inference_mode():
    inputs = {"input_ids": output["input_ids"].cuda(), "attention_mask": output["attention_mask"].cuda()}
    output_embeddings = model(**inputs, output_hidden_states=True, return_last_hidden_state=True).hidden_states[:-1, 0] # get rid of the <eos> token
print(output_embeddings.shape)
PY
steps.explanation: Copied from the model card's How to use block, which loads Bo1015/proteinglm-1b-mlm. Rewire wrapped it in a shell heredoc and added the final print so the step shows a result. The repository README runs the same code against biomap-research/xtrimopglm-100b-int4, which needs an 80GB GPU.

steps.title: Generate a sequence with a causal model
steps.shell:
python3 - <<'PY'
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, AutoConfig
import torch

tokenizer  = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("biomap-research/xtrimopglm-100b-int4", trust_remote_code=True, use_fast=True)
config = AutoConfig.from_pretrained("biomap-research/xtrimopglm-100b-int4",  trust_remote_code=True, torch_dtype=torch.half)
config.is_causal=True
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("biomap-research/xtrimopglm-100b-int4", config = config, torch_dtype=torch.half,trust_remote_code=True)
if torch.cuda.is_available():
    model = model.cuda()
model.eval()

gen_kwargs = {'max_length': 256, 'top_p': 0.8, 'temperature':0.9, "num_beams": 1}
prompt=['', 'MLFVVL', 'LDL', 'VTQA']

for idx, each in enumerate(prompt):
    print(f"Begin generating idx: {idx} with prompt {each}")
    output = model.chat(tokenizer, each, **gen_kwargs)
    print(f"\nEnd generation with length: {len(output.split())} - seqs: {output}\n")
PY

profile.summary: DeepSequence learns a generative model of one protein family from a multiple sequence alignment, with no labels and no experimental measurements. It is a variational autoencoder: the alignment is compressed to a small latent space and decoded back to a distribution over sequences. Once fitted, it scores the effect of a mutation by how much less probable the mutated sequence is than the wild type, and it can also supply features for supervised learning or generate new sequences.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: first paragraph; paper abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A model is fitted to one alignment at a time. The training example builds a VariationalAutoencoder over the alignment: an encoder of two layers of 1500 units, a latent space of 30 dimensions, a decoder of 100 then 500 units, a convolutional final layer of width 40 with 4 patterns, and a sigmoid output with a learned scale. Sequence weights are computed from the alignment before training. The example runs 300,000 stochastic variational inference updates. The published idea is that this nonlinear latent variable model captures dependencies among many residues at once, where pairwise models capture only covariation between pairs.
sections.source_locator: examples/run_svi.py: model_params and train_params; README.md: first paragraph; paper abstract

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There is no versioned release and no checkpoint family. The repository holds one implementation, read at commit fd5c272b, and the fitted parameters are per protein family: the example script downloads pretrained parameters for beta-lactamase, a PDZ domain and PABP. A result must therefore name the alignment, the random seed and the number of updates, not a checkpoint name. The example fixes the seed at 12345 and trains for 300,000 updates on the BLAT_ECOLX alignment.

profile.summary: SaProt is a protein language model whose vocabulary covers structure as well as sequence. Each position is a single token that pairs the amino acid with a Foldseek structure token derived from the 3D structure, so one input string carries both. It was trained by masked language modelling on about 40 million protein sequences and structures. It is used for zero-shot variant effect prediction, for embeddings, and as a starting point for fine-tuning on supervised tasks.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The model is an ESM-style masked language model: the 650M checkpoint has 33 layers, hidden size 1280, 20 attention heads and rotary position embeddings. The difference is the vocabulary of 446 tokens, one per pair of amino acid and Foldseek structure letter, so the string M#EvVpQpL# is read as the tokens M#, Ev, Vp, Qp and L#. A helper calls the Foldseek binary to turn a PDB or mmCIF file into the structure letters. The hash character marks a position whose structure is left out, which the developers advise for AlphaFold2 regions with pLDDT below 70.

sections.body: Four checkpoints are listed: SaProt_35M_AF2 (35M parameters, 40M AF2 structures), SaProt_650M_AF2 (650M, 40M AF2 structures), SaProt_650M_PDB (650M, the same first phase plus 60K PDB structures in a second phase) and SaProt_1.3B_AFDB_OMG_NCBI (1.3B, AF2 structures plus 200M OMG_prot50 and 150M NCBI sequences filtered at 70% identity). profile.summary: MSA Transformer is a protein language model that reads a whole multiple sequence alignment rather than one sequence. Attention runs twice in each layer, once along the rows (the residues of a sequence) and once down the columns (the same position across the aligned sequences), and training was masked language modelling across many protein families. It is used to embed an alignment, to predict residue contacts from its attention maps, and to score variants zero-shot. It is published inside Meta's ESM repository as ESM-MSA-1b, a 12 layer model of about 100M parameters.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper abstract; README.md: Main models you should use; Pre-trained Models table

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The input is a set of aligned sequences. Each layer applies attention along a row and then down a column, so a residue is informed both by the rest of its own sequence and by what sits at the same alignment position in the family. Training masks residues and predicts them, across many families at once, rather than fitting one model per family. For contact prediction the tied row attention maps are read by a logistic regression, the same method used for the single-sequence ESM models. For variant scoring the repository's program masks each position of the first sequence in the alignment in turn and reads the log probability of each amino acid there, a strategy it calls masked marginals, which is the only strategy it allows for this model.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two checkpoints exist. ESM-MSA-1 was released with the February 2021 preprint. ESM-MSA-1b followed in July 2021 with what the developers call a minor fix in the row positional embeddings, and is the one the README recommends. Both are 12 layers, about 100M parameters, embedding dimension 768, trained on UR50/S with alignments from the 2018_03 release. A result must name which of the two was used, and also the alignment and how deeply it was sampled, because the scoring program takes only the first 400 sequences of the alignment by default.

profile.summary: HyPLM-Flash is a masked protein language model of 652 million parameters. It reads one amino acid sequence, up to 8,190 residues in a single window, and returns a 1280-dimensional vector per residue, a pooled vector, or masked language model logits that can be turned into a zero-shot variant score. It keeps the 33 token alphabet and the output head of ESM-2, so it can stand in for ESM-2 in an existing pipeline, and it ships with its own GPU inference engine that uses INT8 matrix multiplication and padding-free batching.
profile.summary_source_locator: Report abstract and Section 2.1; README.md: Usage

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: It is a bidirectional transformer encoder trained by masked language modelling: 15 per cent of residues are selected, 80 per cent of those replaced by a mask token, 10 per cent by a random amino acid and 10 per cent left as they are. Each of the 32 blocks puts RMSNorm before self-attention with per-head query and key normalisation and rotary positions, then before a SwiGLU feed-forward layer, each inside a residual connection. The output head is RoBERTa style: a dense layer, GELU, LayerNorm, then a linear map to 33 logits. The block weights were trained with the Muon optimiser and everything else with AdamW.
sections.source_locator: Report Section 2.1 and Section 2.2 (Objective and optimization); weights/config.json

sections.title: Training data and decontamination
sections.body: The corpus combines UniRef90 with the UniRef50 representatives it does not contain, MGnify90, the active entries of UniParc and the non-redundant isolate proteomes of JGI IMG. Sequences of 30 to 8,192 residues are kept, exact duplicates are removed across sources, and the sequences of the benchmarks used during development are removed by exact match, including all ProteinGym wild types and variants. That leaves 2.6 billion sequences, or 659 billion residues, sampled in proportion to length, so metagenomic and archival sequences supply about 80 per cent of the tokens. Pretraining covers 713 billion tokens on crops of up to 1,022 residues; a second stage of 13 billion tokens extends the crops to 8,190 residues and adds auxiliary structure objectives on 1.6 million chains, with those chains first filtered against the test proteins by MMseqs2. The auxiliary heads are used only during training.
sections.source_locator: Report Section 2.2: Data, Training stages, Training compute

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One checkpoint is released, version 1.0.0 of the hyplm package, with the report dated 12 October 2026. The 2.6 GB of FP32 weights come as two shards from the repository's GitHub Releases under the tag hyplm-flash-weights; the download script merges them and checks the sha256 against ce7dcd4fc473dc334d869718a9a31149573893795db03c45efeb396e8b180ab1. A result must also name the precision, because the engine runs INT8 by default and BF16 on request. The developers state that zero-shot, structure, function and likelihood metrics agree within 0.01 between the two, while representations of variants of the same protein differ by about 1 per cent, so they advise BF16 when training regressors on such data.

encoder = HyPLMEncoder.from_pretrained("weights")

profile.summary: CMLM designs an amino acid sequence for a protein backbone that is given to it (inverse folding). It is the non-autoregressive ProteinMPNN baseline of the ByProt codebase: a ProteinMPNN-style graph encoder and decoder trained by conditional masked language modelling, so at generation time it predicts every position at once from one categorical distribution rather than one residue after another. The released checkpoint is called protein_mpnn_cmlm and was trained on CATH 4.2.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The model is ProteinMPNN's message-passing encoder and decoder, trained with a conditional masked language modelling objective instead of left-to-right prediction. Generation uses the mask-predict strategy with one decoding iteration by default, so all positions are filled in a single parallel pass. The ByProt defaults make this explicit: max_iter is 1 and the strategy is mask_predict for ProtMPNN-CMLM, against 5 iterations and denoising for LM-Design. Sampling temperature defaults to 0, which makes the output deterministic.

profile.summary: DPLM-2 is a protein language model that handles sequence and structure in one model. Backbone coordinates are turned into discrete tokens by a quantising structure tokeniser, so a protein becomes one token string of amino acids and structure tokens, and a discrete diffusion language model is trained over both. From that single model come sequence and structure co-generation, folding (structure from sequence), inverse folding (sequence from structure) and motif scaffolding. Checkpoints are released at 150M, 650M and 3B parameters, plus a bit-based variant.
profile.summary_source_locator: arXiv abstract; model card: first paragraphs and Model Details

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The 650M checkpoint is an ESM-style transformer with 33 layers, hidden size 1280 and 20 attention heads, loaded by the class EsmForDPLM2. What makes it multimodal is the vocabulary: 8,229 tokens covering amino acids, structure tokens and special tokens. Structure tokens come from a separate structure tokeniser, published as airkingbd/struct_tokenizer, which also rebuilds a PDB file from tokens. Training is discrete diffusion over this joint vocabulary, and it starts from a pretrained DPLM sequence model, a warm-up strategy the authors use to carry evolutionary knowledge into structure modelling. The README adds that DPLM-2 does inverse folding by conditioning directly on structure tokens, where the earlier DPLM used an adapter on top of the language model.
sections.source_locator: Model card: Model Details; config.json; arXiv abstract; README.md: Structure-conditioned generation

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Four checkpoints answered on Hugging Face: dplm2_150m, dplm2_650m, dplm2_3b and dplm2_bit_650m, the last being the finer-grained bit-based variant from the follow-up work the authors call DPLM-2.1. All are Apache-2.0 and none is gated. Decoding settings matter as much as the checkpoint: the README's inverse folding and folding commands use 100 iterations with deterministic unmasking and argmax sampling, and a July 2025 note says the default sampling strategy of DPLM-2 was changed to annealing@2.0:0.1. The HyInv report evaluated DPLM-2 3B at argmax decoding over 100 steps in BF16 autocast, and notes that with deterministic unmasking two designs of the same chain are almost always the same sequence.

sections.body: Training uses experimental structures from the PDB together with AlphaFold2 predicted structures from SwissProt, published as the preprocessed dataset airkingbd/pdb_swissprot. The model is initialised from a pretrained DPLM checkpoint, and LoRA is used to keep the parameters from shifting far, with about 64,000 tokens per batch for 100,000 training steps. The bit-based variant uses the same data.

profile.summary: LigandMPNN designs amino acid sequences for a protein backbone that is given to it, and unlike earlier methods of its kind it also reads the non-protein atoms around that backbone: small molecules, nucleotides and metals. The input is a PDB file, the output a set of designed sequences with per-sequence confidence figures, and optionally packed side chain conformations so binding interactions can be inspected. The published package also serves ProteinMPNN, SolubleMPNN and two membrane-labelled models from the same code.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper abstract; README.md: first paragraph, Available models

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Design is autoregressive over the backbone graph, in the manner of ProteinMPNN, with the ligand atoms added as context. The LigandMPNN checkpoints are built with 32 neighbour edges and 25 context atoms per residue, which is what the names ligandmpnn_v_32_005_25 and the like record. The atom context can be switched off with a flag, which the README offers as a way to see how much the ligand atoms move the amino acid probabilities, and side chain context can be switched on. A separate side chain packing checkpoint produces the side chain conformations.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Available models, examples 21 and 22, Side chain packing model; get_model_params.sh comments

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Four LigandMPNN checkpoints are published, differing in the Gaussian coordinate noise used in training: 0.05, 0.10, 0.20 and 0.30 Angstrom. The same download script also fetches four ProteinMPNN checkpoints, four SolubleMPNN checkpoints, two membrane-labelled models and the side chain packing model, all from files.ipd.uw.edu. A result must name the checkpoint, the model type, the sampling temperature and the seed, since the README is explicit that no seed means a random seed and that running again gives different results. The default model type of run.py is ProteinMPNN, not LigandMPNN.

profile.summary: LM-Design designs an amino acid sequence for a protein backbone that is given to it (inverse folding). Rather than training a structure model from scratch, it takes an existing protein language model and implants a lightweight structural adapter into it, so the language model's knowledge of natural sequences is reused and given awareness of the fold. At generation time the sequence is refined over several passes. The released checkpoints are built on ESM-1b 650M and ESM-2 650M and trained on CATH 4.2, with one multichain checkpoint for complexes.
profile.summary_source_locator: arXiv abstract; ByProt README.md: Official implementation of LM-Design, Pretrained model weights

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A structural adapter is added to a frozen protein language model, which is what the authors call structural surgery. Generation is iterative: the ByProt defaults for LM-Design are five decoding iterations with the denoise strategy, against one iteration and mask_predict for the non-autoregressive ProteinMPNN baseline in the same repository. Sampling temperature defaults to 0, which makes the output deterministic; the README shows how to override it. The HyInv report describes the model's decoding as iterative denoising in five steps.
sections.source_locator: arXiv abstract; ByProt README.md: flags for generation, Example 2; HyInv report Table 5

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Three LM-Design checkpoints are published in Zenodo deposit 10046338 of 27 October 2023: lm_design_esm1b_650m on CATH 4.2, lm_design_esm2_650m on CATH 4.2, and lm_design_esm2_650m trained on the multichain data for complexes. Each archive is about 1.6 GB. The repository also holds experiment configurations for the ESM-2 series under configs/experiment/fixedbb, but only the 650M checkpoints are released. A result must name the base language model, the training data and the decoding settings, since five iterations at temperature 0 is not the same run as five iterations at temperature 0.1.

The repository's own worked example recovers 0.76 of the native sequence on one backbone, against 0.37 for the CMLM baseline. Separately, the HyInv report used LM-Design 650M as one of ten published baselines and puts its own model ahead by 0.044 scTM on average, while noting that LM-Design is among the parallel decoders that sample at lower diversity. profile.summary: RhoMax predicts the wavelength of light a microbial rhodopsin absorbs most strongly, from its amino acid sequence alone. The sequence is first folded by AlphaFold2, then the 24 residues that line the retinal binding pocket are cut out and turned into a graph: one node per atom, an edge between atoms within 2 Angstrom. A small graph neural network reads that graph and returns one number, the absorption maximum in nanometres. The purpose is to find red-shifted rhodopsins for optogenetics without measuring each candidate.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Method Summary

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The sequence is folded with AlphaFold2, run with default parameters and without templates, and the highest-ranked model is kept; the authors measure a median RMSD of 1.08 Angstrom against the crystal structures they could check. A multiple sequence alignment picks out the 24 binding pocket residues. Each atom of those residues becomes a node with a feature vector of spatial and chemical properties, and atoms within 2 Angstrom are joined by an edge whose features come from the distance. The network is four graph layers: graph convolution, two graph attention layers, then graph convolution, each without self-loops and with one attention head, followed by batch normalisation and an ELU activation, with mean aggregation at the end to give a single number. It is designed to be invariant to rigid motions of the structure.

The authors publish the data sets, the source code and a Colab notebook in one GitHub repository, whose default branch is colab and which was last pushed in November 2024. The paper computes four train and test splits, and the repository holds a single pickled model under predict/. profile.summary: AMPLIFY is a protein language model. It reads a protein amino acid sequence and returns per-residue and per-protein embeddings and masked-token logits, which can be used as features for property prediction or to suggest mutations. It comes in two sizes, 120M and 350M parameters, and the authors released the training code, data and checkpoints.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: AMPLIFY is a transformer encoder trained with masked language modelling: 15% of residues are masked and the model learns to predict them. The layers use rotary position embeddings, SwiGLU activations and RMS normalisation, with no bias terms in the attention or feed-forward layers. Training ran in two stages. Stage 1 ran for 1,000,000 steps on sequences of up to 512 residues. Stage 2 extended the length to 2048 for 25,000 steps (120M) or 50,000 steps (350M). The authors frame the work around data quality rather than scale: they argue that sequence databases are a biased sample of the fitness landscape and built a curated training set, UR100P.

The two sizes differ in width and depth (640 hidden units and 24 layers against 960 and 32). profile.summary: ProstT5 is a protein language model that translates between a protein's amino acid sequence and a one-letter-per-residue description of its 3D structure (Foldseek 3Di tokens). Given a sequence it can predict 3Di tokens ('folding'), given 3Di tokens it can propose sequences ('inverse folding'), and its encoder gives per-residue and per-protein embeddings of either. The authors use the predicted 3Di strings for fast structure-based search with Foldseek without computing 3D structures.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ProstT5 is a T5 encoder-decoder initialised from ProtT5-XL-U50, a model trained with span corruption on protein sequences. Structures are written as Foldseek 3Di strings, which assign each residue one of twenty structural states. Training had two steps. First the model continued the span-denoising objective on both amino acid and 3Di sequences, to learn the new tokens without forgetting amino acids. Then it was trained to translate in both directions. A prefix token sets the direction: <AA2fold> for sequence to 3Di and <fold2AA> for 3Di to sequence. 3Di letters are written in lower case so they do not clash with amino acid letters.

sections.body: The training set was built from AlphaFoldDB predictions: clusters were expanded with diverse members, then low-confidence predictions (pLDDT below 70), proteins shorter than 30 residues and highly repetitive 3Di strings were removed. The final set has 17M proteins, which gives 34M training samples because each protein is used in both translation directions. Training first truncated sequences to 256 residues and later extended to 512.

steps.title: Compute embeddings
steps.shell:
python3 - <<'PY'
from transformers import T5Tokenizer, T5EncoderModel
import torch
import re
device = torch.device('cuda:0' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu')

tokenizer = T5Tokenizer.from_pretrained('Rostlab/ProstT5', do_lower_case=False)
model = T5EncoderModel.from_pretrained("Rostlab/ProstT5").to(device)
model.float() if device.type=='cpu' else model.half()

sequence_examples = ["PRTEINO", "strct"]
sequence_examples = [" ".join(list(re.sub(r"[UZOB]", "X", sequence))) for sequence in sequence_examples]
sequence_examples = [ "<AA2fold>" + " " + s if s.isupper() else "<fold2AA>" + " " + s
                      for s in sequence_examples
                    ]

ids = tokenizer.batch_encode_plus(sequence_examples,
                                  add_special_tokens=True,
                                  padding="longest",
                                  return_tensors='pt').to(device)

with torch.no_grad():
    embedding_repr = model(
              ids.input_ids,
              attention_mask=ids.attention_mask
              )

emb_0 = embedding_repr.last_hidden_state[0,1:8] # shape (7 x 1024)
emb_1 = embedding_repr.last_hidden_state[1,1:6] # shape (5 x 1024)
emb_0_per_protein = emb_0.mean(dim=0) # shape (1024)
PY

profile.summary: FrameDiff generates new protein backbones from noise. It represents each residue as a rigid body (a frame: a position and an orientation in 3D) and runs a diffusion model over those frames. The output is a set of monomer backbone structures in PDB format at the requested lengths, which can then be given sequences with a design tool such as ProteinMPNN.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The authors develop a diffusion model on SE(3), the space of rotations and translations, applied to one frame per residue. Noise is added separately to translations (an R(3) diffuser) and rotations (an SO(3) diffuser), and a network learns the SE(3) equivariant score used to reverse the noise. In the released configuration the score network has 4 blocks of invariant point attention layers with 8 heads and a 2-layer sequence transformer, node embedding 256 and edge embedding 128. The repository keeps a modified fork of OpenFold. FrameDiff does not rely on a pretrained structure prediction network. Sampling uses 500 steps by default.

profile.summary: ProtTrans is a family of protein language models from Rostlab, trained on unlabelled protein sequences from UniRef and BFD. The models take an amino acid sequence and return per-residue vectors (1024 values each for ProtT5-XL), which are averaged for a per-protein vector; those vectors are then used as the only input to small supervised models for tasks such as secondary structure or subcellular localisation. The family covers six architectures, and ProtT5-XL-UniRef50 is the one the authors recommend.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each model is a standard NLP transformer trained on protein sequences with no labels. The authors trained two autoregressive models (Transformer-XL and XLNet) and four autoencoder models (BERT, Albert, Electra and T5). ProtT5-XL-UniRef50 follows the t5-3b shape, with model width 1024, 24 encoder and 24 decoder layers and 32 heads, but is trained with a Bart-like masked language modelling objective rather than T5 span denoising, masking 15% of amino acids. Sequences are uppercased, the rare amino acids U, Z, O and B are mapped to X, and residues are separated by single spaces. For feature extraction the authors recommend the encoder side only.

profile.summary: AlphaPeptDeep (package name peptdeep) is a Python framework for predicting properties of peptides from their sequence. Its built-in pretrained models take a peptide sequence, its modifications, precursor charge, collision energy and instrument type, and predict the MS2 fragment intensities, the retention time and the collision cross section. The usual output is a predicted spectral library, for example built from a FASTA file, for use in peptide identification.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: About; paper: abstract and introduction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The MS2 model is built on four transformer layers with a hidden size of 256. For each peptide of length n it outputs intensities for (n-1) cleavage positions and eight fragment types: singly and doubly charged b and y ions and their modification-associated neutral losses. The retention time and collision cross section models are smaller: a CNN layer followed by two bidirectional LSTM layers. Modifications are represented by their chemical composition, so a modification the model has not seen can still be encoded. Training intensities are normalised by the highest matched intensity in each spectrum, so predictions lie between zero and one. The authors stress transfer learning: refining a pretrained model takes minutes and is possible without a GPU.

sections.body: The pretrained models are not versioned as separate checkpoints on the page: peptdeep downloads a single pretrained_models.zip from the repository's pre-trained-models release when it is first used, and the settings file names its URL in model_url. The MS2 model has several variants selected by model_type, which can be generic, phos, hla or digly, and separate releases exist for other labels, for example dimethyl-labelled peptides. External model files can be given instead with external_ms2_model, external_rt_model and external_ccs_model. A result should name the peptdeep version and the model type; this page read the repository at commit 8e9eba6e.

profile.summary: FastSpel predicts the fragment intensities of a tryptic peptide measured by higher-energy collisional dissociation, so that a spectral library can be generated or peptide-spectrum matches rescored. It takes a list of precursors, each with a modified sequence, a precursor charge and a collision energy, and returns the non-zero predicted b and y ion intensities with their m/z values. Instead of a neural network it fits a separate multistep linear regression for each peptide length, charge and collision energy, which makes it fast and its parameters readable.
profile.summary_source_locator: paper: abstract, Description of FastSpel Prediction Method; download page: Spectral library generation

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: For each combination of peptide length, precursor charge and collision energy, FastSpel fits a multistep linear regression that maps a binary encoding of the peptide sequence to the fragment intensity profile. Peptides are built from the 20 common amino acids plus oxidised methionine, so the encoding uses 21 symbols, and fragments are predicted up to charge min(3, precursor charge). The model is effectively hundreds of small separate models: the paper says 350 length, charge and collision energy triplets were trained. Because the relation is linear, the authors read the fitted coefficients and find known fragmentation rules such as the proline effect.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The code is a Python package distributed from the group's own site, not from GitHub or PyPI. The FTP folder it links to holds one file, fastspel-0.1.0.tar.gz, and the page's install commands name that same version. The page says it was last updated on 2 September 2026. A result should name the package version and the collision energy used, because a separate model is fitted per collision energy and only the six trained values are accepted.

profile.summary: PredFull predicts a complete tandem mass spectrum for a peptide, not only the b and y fragment ions. The input is a table of peptides with precursor charge, fragmentation type (HCD or ETD) and normalised collision energy; the output is an MGF file of predicted peaks. The model is a residual convolutional network that predicts intensity in mass bins of 0.1 Th up to m/z 2000.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: PredFull treats the spectrum as a vector of mass bins rather than a list of named fragment ions. The script sets a bin width of 0.1 Th and a spectrum dimension of 20000 bins, which covers m/z up to 2000. The network is built from residual convolutional blocks, with coordinate channels added to the convolutions so position information is available, and it is trained on over 2 million experimental spectra. Predicted peaks weaker than one thousandth of the strongest peak are dropped as noise.

profile.summary: Prosit Transformer predicts MS2 fragment intensities for a peptide using a transformer instead of the recurrent network of the original Prosit. It takes a peptide sequence with its precursor charge and collision energy and predicts the intensities of the six common ion series (singly, doubly and triply charged b and y ions). It is built by putting a prediction head on TAPE, a transformer trained on protein sequences, and fine-tuning it on the Prosit training data.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: TAPE is a transformer autoencoder trained on Pfam protein sequences to fill in a missing residue. It has 12 attention layers of 768 hidden units and encodes the peptide into a 512-dimensional embedding. A Prosit-specific transformer with the same settings but nine attention layers decodes the combined embedding. A separate metadata layer, a two-layer perceptron of width 512, takes seven inputs: a six-dimensional one-hot charge state and the collision energy. Its output is combined with the peptide embedding before the decoder, and a two-layer prediction layer follows the decoder. Predicted negative intensities are set to zero, and ions that cannot exist for a peptide, because the charge or the length is too low, are set to -1 and excluded from similarity measurements.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The code is in the first author's repository, which has no licence file and no release. It installs with pip install -e . and uses the TAPE training command, and the README's notes say that downloading trained models is still a to-do, so no weights are published there. The training data are the Prosit HDF5 files from figshare, converted to LMDB; the paper says the converted LMDB files were deposited on figshare as well. A result therefore has to state which model the author trained and with which config file; the repository's example config is config/prositTransformer.json. profile.summary: UniSpec predicts the full set of fragment ion series for a peptide, not only b and y ions, and is sensitive to the collision energy. The input is a spectrum label: sequence, charge, modifications and collision energy. The output is a predicted intensity for each entry of a fixed fragment dictionary, written out as an msp spectral library. The released model, UniSpec23, ships in the repository with its dictionary and accessory files.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: UniSpec predicts into a fixed dictionary of fragment ions rather than a binned spectrum. The released model config has 9 blocks, an embedding size of 256, 38 input channels, a sequence length of 40 and an output dimension of 7919, which is the size of the fragment dictionary. Attention head sizes are 16, 16 and 64, and the last filter width is 512. The training config has an option CEembed for embedding the collision energy; in the released UniSpec23 config it is false. A dictionary usage criteria file and ion statistics from training ship beside the checkpoint and are used when a prediction is written.
